posts.title: A Mac guard for AI coding tools
posts.promise: See and control what coding agents can access on a Mac.
posts.whatItIs: Plango describes a Mac security product with controls for coding agent access, MCP servers, skills and plugins, plus secret handling and connection monitoring. A beginner could hypothetically prototype a narrow checklist that helps a Mac user review agent permissions; it would not itself secure the computer.
posts.whoPays: Plango advertises a subscription. A separate beginner checklist service would need to test whether Mac developers would pay; that demand is only a hypothesis.
loop: User lists the coding agents and folders they use.
A form asks which files or connections they want to restrict.
A simple rules checklist maps answers to review prompts.
The user checks the suggestions against actual Mac settings.
A person approves every access change and tests it manually.
posts.evidence: Plango's site describes agent access controls, MCP server visibility, skill and plugin checks, moving plain text keys into Keychain, connection monitoring and Mac requirements. It lists $4.99 per month and a seven day free trial.
posts.uncertainty: These are claims on Plango's own site, not independently verified outcomes. The proposed checklist is hypothetical and cannot inspect or protect a Mac automatically; a person must verify settings and avoid exposing secrets.
first24Hours: Read Plango's feature and system requirement pages.
Draft a one page checklist for reviewing one coding agent's file access.
Ask one Mac developer to check whether the prompts are understandable; do not request credentials or sensitive files.

ease.reason: A permission checklist is a small first experiment, though useful Mac security guidance requires careful domain learning.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: Mac developers might pay for clearer agent permission reviews; the source lists Plango pricing but does not validate demand for a checklist.

feasibility.reason: A static checklist can be prototyped in four weeks, but the source's access controls and protection claims are beyond that narrow version.

autonomy.reason: A form can organize answers, while users must verify settings and approve every security change.

evidence.reason: The first party site describes the working product and features, but supplies no independent real use evidence.

posts.title: Turn project notes into a reviewed brief
posts.promise: Try a local assistant workflow that drafts a project brief for you to check.
posts.whatItIs: Kucedr presents a desktop assistant for writing, research, coding and media tasks, with local files, configurable model providers and scheduled tasks that require the app to stay open. Its site shows a demo saving an artwork selection, copy, layout and palette as a brief. A student could hypothetically test a similar brief-making workflow with sample notes.
posts.whoPays: Kucedr offers downloads and says its cloud service is coming soon. A student version's buyer and willingness to pay are hypothetical and untested.
loop: Choose a fictional project and provide non-sensitive notes.
Ask the assistant to extract the project name, goal and open questions.
Generate a short brief with those fields and source notes.
Compare every field with the original notes.
Edit or discard unsupported details before sharing the brief.
posts.evidence: Kucedr's site describes a desktop assistant for macOS, Linux and Windows, configurable providers, local profile and files, and scheduled tasks that run while Kucedr remains open. Its embedded example shows saving artwork, copy, layout and palette into a brief, with date and venue still to add.
posts.uncertainty: The product details and example come from Kucedr's own site. The example does not establish accuracy across other projects. The student workflow is hypothetical; a person must check facts, privacy and missing details before sharing or scheduling anything.
first24Hours: Review Kucedr's getting started information and supported desktop platforms.
Use fictional notes to outline a five field project brief.
Manually compare a draft brief with its sample notes and mark any unsupported or missing fields.

ease.reason: The site describes a desktop workflow and a concrete saved brief demo that a beginner can inspect and imitate with sample notes.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: people coordinating small projects might value brief drafting, but the source gives no evidence of paying customers or demand for this adaptation.

feasibility.reason: A draft-and-review brief using sample notes fits a four-week experiment; trustworthy integration across users' tools would be a larger task.

autonomy.reason: Drafting can be repeated from notes, but the source's example leaves date and venue incomplete and a human must check content.

evidence.reason: The first party page describes the product and shows a working brief example, but does not establish outside use or accuracy.

posts.title: Review search results before an agent uses them
posts.promise: Explore a search workflow with a human review step built in.
posts.whatItIs: Gsearch's repository describes a self-hosted MCP server that uses Firefox to retrieve Google results for AI agents, including resolved result URLs and typed JSON. A beginner could hypothetically prototype a manual research log that records search questions and lets a person check links before use. The prototype would not automate Google access.
posts.whoPays: The repository describes Gsearch as self-hosted and says no API key is required. Whether developers would pay for a separate reviewed research workflow is hypothetical and untested.
loop: Write a research question and record its purpose.
Run a search only after checking applicable service terms and access rules.
Record the returned result titles and destination URLs.
Open each candidate page and check that it supports the intended point.
A person decides which source, if any, an agent may use.
posts.evidence: The repository README describes Gsearch as a self-hosted Google search MCP using Firefox and returning results as typed JSON. It documents a live-call demonstration and cautions that automated Google access may breach Google's Terms of Service.
posts.uncertainty: These are repository claims and demonstrations, not independent checks of reliability or permission. Google access has an explicit terms risk. The proposed manual log does not automate searches; people must confirm terms, inspect pages and reject unsupported or unsafe material.
first24Hours: Read the repository's legal and responsible use section before considering live use.
Create a manual research log template with question, result URL and support notes.
Populate it using saved or otherwise permitted example material and have a person verify each claim against its page.

ease.reason: A manual research log is approachable, but the documented live workflow requires installing a browser-based server and careful terms review.

profit.reason: Hypothesis: developers might value reviewed research notes, but the repository offers no evidence of paying demand for that service.

feasibility.reason: A manual log and review prototype fits four weeks; automating live Google searches carries a terms risk the README explicitly flags.

autonomy.reason: The safe proposed log is mostly manual, and a person must verify sources and decide what an agent can use.

evidence.reason: The repository gives implementation details and a live-call demonstration, while its claims are first-party and do not establish independent real use.
